text: This final piece of calculus review brings together complex numbers and the exponential function: e to the i theta, the complex exponential, is the mathematical object behind every phase you'll ever encounter in a quantum circuit.

Euler's formula states e to the i theta equals cosine theta plus i sine theta. Verified numerically at theta equals pi over 4, both cosine and sine come out to roughly 0.7071 — the same one-over-root-two value you've already seen repeatedly as the Hadamard gate's amplitude, now appearing as the real and imaginary parts of a complex exponential. That's not a coincidence — rotation gates are literally built from complex exponentials.

For a real exponent, e to the x grows without bound. For a purely imaginary exponent, something completely different happens: since cosine squared plus sine squared always equals 1, the point stays at distance exactly 1 from the origin, no matter the angle. As theta increases, e to the i theta doesn't grow at all — it just moves around the unit circle. A phase is a position on that circle, not a magnitude.

The phase gates S and T are built exactly this way, multiplying the ket-one amplitude by a specific point on the unit circle — shifting its phase while leaving its magnitude, and therefore its measurement probability, completely unchanged. And a quantum state evolving under a constant energy for time t picks up a phase factor of the same form, e to the negative i H t over h-bar — the same identity, now with the Hamiltonian operator in the exponent, producing the oscillating behavior of a quantum state over time.

The final lesson of this course applies every tool you've built — vectors, matrices, complex numbers, eigenvalues, unitary operators, tensor products, probability, and complex exponentials — to one real, small quantum circuit, traced through completely by hand.
